The Wronskian $W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)$ of two vector-valued functions 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/e61be508e4ad25ed39996a7a924a732290f3c8be7e5e953e01da6ff35c5669f4.png)
is defined as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/ed9d2deba98ee27ebe8a183cab45f42a92f2d4f49733fa8a8f7c9acdf6185912.png)

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are linearly independent.

- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/3ac4270c91e71468086149ed819c644c71d59aea898520acc8e5fbf30205985c.png)

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/7d502d9256ace32899ea72f143f3694db8f0531efebf2dbd0c20dc857bd563b5.png) $\text{isn't}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}({t}^{2}+1)^{′} \\ (-4t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+1 \\ -4t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2t \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+1\cdot (-4t) \\ -4\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)+(-2)\cdot (-4t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2t \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}-4t+2 \\ -4{t}^{2}+8t-4\end{aligned}]\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/c223cfc85f5a1f23006dd9de1775f898731a2cce2b88d1c27c0ab3f4ee238e66.png) $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(2t+1)^{′} \\ (-4t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t+1 \\ -4t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (2t+1)+1\cdot (-4t) \\ -4\cdot (2t+1)+(-2)\cdot (-4t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066416/assets/2f5d5dd7f1fe1b1a51df2930d780fc11af9a31f8cac9cc9c38f966eb42bc848d.png) $\text{is}$ a solution of the system. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}(t)^{′} \\ (1-2t)^{′}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ 1-2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot t+1\cdot (1-2t) \\ -4\cdot t+(-2)\cdot (1-2t)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the set of solutions $\big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}.$ Its Wronskian is

$$
\begin{aligned}W(b,c) & =|\begin{aligned}2t+1 & t \\ -4t & 1-2t\end{aligned}| \\  & =(2t+1)\cdot (1-2t)-t\cdot (-4t) \\  & =(2t+1)(1-2t)+4{t}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $t \in \mathbb R.$ Thus, since $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one $t\in\mathbb R,$ $\big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}$ is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.
